utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First of all, good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-02-60-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic, Dragan Obrenovic, Dragan Jokic, and Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And may we have the appearances for the Office of the Prosecutor, please. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. My name is Peter McCloskey and today with me are Stacy de la Torre and Melissa Epstein, and the case manager, Janet Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence for Mr. Obrenovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours, my name is David Wilson with Dusan Slijepcevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please take the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I am David Wilson, counsel for Obrenovic, seated at the table with Mr. Dusan Slijepcevic, who is co-counsel for Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. President and Your Honours. Michael Karnavas for Mr. Blagojevic, and with me is Suzana Tomanovic, my legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. For Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MS. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Miodrag Stojanovic, Defence counsel for Dragan Jokic, and with me is my co-counsel Cynthia Sinatra. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On channel 4 we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Now we have French on channel 4, but probably we can continue. And it's now Defence counsel for Mr. Nikolic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I am Veselin Londrovic, appearing for Mr. Momir Nikolic, and my co-counsel, Stefan Kirsch, is also appearing for Momir Nikolic, and Ms. Vesna Anic is helping us with interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this. Then I learned that we have today, and we all appreciate this very much, representatives acting under Rule 74 as amici curiae, friends of the Court. May I please ask you for your names and your capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Trivun Jovicic. I am an advisor of the Ministry in the Embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKOVAC
utterances.text: I am a Minister consul, charge d'affaires of Bosnia-Herzegovina here in the Netherlands, and I'm working here as a mandatory of the Presidency in this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much for coming and assisting the Court. We now turn to the main persons of this case and this, of course, is the accused. May I, first of all, ask the three of them being present here whether they can understand me in a language they understand, and at the same time already now whether there are any observations as regards their health condition and their situation in the Detention Unit. Mr. Obrenovic, please. THE ACCUSED OBRENOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do hear and understand in my own language what is being spoken in the courtroom. I have no objections to the conditions of detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Blagojevic. THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do understand. I have no complaint against the conditions of detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphone be switched on, please. THE ACCUSED NIKOLIC: [Interpretation] I hear and understand in my own language. I have no complaints against the conditions in the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this. As you can see from the scheduling order, the intention is first to have a relatively brief Status Conference. We are obliged to have this Status Conference 120 days after the -- after either the initial appearance or the last Status Conference. And therefore this Status Conference is due today. In preparation of our hearing today, the parties met with the senior legal officer in this case and discussed procedural issues. Some have not yet been resolved; others can be probably resolved within the next minutes. Later, without a break, we'll go immediately over to the hearings on provisional release as regards Mr. Obrenovic and Mr. Blagojevic. If I understood correctly, one major problem addressed yesterday in the Pre-Trial Conference was -- in the preparing of this hearing now was matters related to 66(B), as regards those statements. We are aware that our sister Tribunal, the Appeals Chamber, made a ruling on 66(B). Unfortunately until to date, it was not possible for us to receive the decision in writing because it was an oral decision, and we didn't have the transcripts until now. The OTP, the question I may ask to you, do you have already access to the decision, and does it change your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have not yet had access to any written decision or any transcript of the oral decision, though I did get a reliable account from the OTP appellate lawyers, and it appears clear to me from that account that the Appellate Chamber defined 66(B) as including witness statements under documents, which was the main thrust of the litigation. And as such, as I said yesterday, it is our purpose now to provide the Defence with all material witness statements for their inspection, and we are in the process of putting those -- that material on searchable CDs and hope to have that accomplished within a few weeks. And as for the actual formal response to -- I would like to have a written order before we withdraw our motion or concede the motion or decide what exactly we do with our motion. But for practical purposes, it appears that it has been clearly decided and that there's no reason to stop the discovery that we have now planned to provide that material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for these comments. Anything else as regards this point only? I can't see anything. Then let me address when it comes to the question of disclosure on the one concern emanating from previous cases. The Bench would really appreciate that we have access to the same documents that the parties have in their possession. It's extremely difficult for Judges to decide on a more or less virtual basis, having not the facts before us. And I heard that some documents will be provided on a CD. And please provide also this Trial Chamber with these documents. Let me now turn to questions --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you will allow me to address the Court, I just wanted to clear this up. The Court wants the Prosecution to disclose to the Chamber all witness statements that the Defence receives?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The major part, especially when it comes down to a CD. And sometimes it's really necessary for the basis of our rulings and decisions, especially on the question of relevance of the one or other document. And when we have later dispute whether or not the one or other should be disclosed or not disclosed, in addition, then we have a better basis for our decision. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: If there's no contest about disclosure, if the Prosecution has already stipulated that he will turn over the witness statements to the Defence, is that still presented to the Chambers for a decision?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we have had in the past extremely good experience working together with the OTP and the parties on these issues, and we got the necessary on the basis of such an informal request.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the only thing I'm considering is it's the decision of the Defence and the decision of the Prosecution what evidence they will use in their case in chief to present to the Trial Chamber. So we receive all of the statements, and I thought it was like a filter as to what we decided to present to the Trial Chamber. But if the procedure is different at this point, then I'm just trying to make sure I'm clear on it. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Now we are discussing only those material disclosed by the OTP. Please understand the general concept of this Tribunal, and here, it is the necessity to come as close as possible to the truth. And this also means that what is usual, for example in your legal system, cannot translate it one to one in our system here, when we are mandated to find the truth, or to search the truth, knowing very well that there is not the one truth. But we need some factual basis. I think it was done probably in the past in other cases, so it should be here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Very briefly that we can expedite the proceedings, I have before me one motion, the Prosecution motion for variation from page limits from 10 to 11. I think it's not worthwhile really discussing, and I can't see any objections to this. And therefore, this motion is granted. We have numerous other motions before us. And I think it was already discussed yesterday that in general, these decisions will not be provided for you before September. This brings me already now - I come back, if necessary, to the point of disclosure later - the time schedule. I know that in the past we envisaged already twice an earlier start of this case. Unfortunately, the reality of the Tribunal always brings new surprises and some cases are a little bit belated, but you should be assured that within Trial Chamber II, the second priority is given to the case before us. Therefore, even in a worst case scenario, the trial of this case can start in May next year. But we have to be prepared. We have to have this trial ready by the end of this year, because I said it's dependent on the development in the Stakic case and there it's only the worst case scenario to finalise in May. I hope and I am still optimistic that we can come there further to a finalisation of this case. Therefore, it is necessary to -- within the schedule, to come to a solution bringing us to the end of this year with all disclosure and additional material. One point here seems for me the Butler report, the Butler report playing an extremely important role in the Krstic case already, and I understood that this Butler report should be updated for the purposes of this case. I think it's necessary to do it as soon as possible, and taking into account that the pre-trial brief should be ready the 1st of November, which is All Saints', but hopefully doesn't mean anything for the case, the 1st of November. At the end of October in this context, the Butler and the updated Butler report should not only be finalised but disclosed to the parties and provided to the Bench. I think this is a reasonable time schedule for the parties. If not, please let me know. Then, as mentioned, pre-trial brief 1st of November, reply by the Defence 25 November, and then immediately in the beginning of the next year, we should have a Pre-Trial Conference. I believe that from the point of view of today this should be a reasonable time schedule. It is our obligation to invite the parties to come as soon as possible to agreed facts or judicial notice or other means of coming together and limiting the contested areas to the absolutely necessary. I can't go today into any details, but I believe it's mandatory for this trial and for the function of this trial that not in each and every trial all the chapeau elements of crime have to be addressed and proven once again on the basis of the witnesses heard already in earlier cases. May I ask the parties now: Are there any problems related to the disclosure of material under Rule 66 or Rule 68?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might. I would like to, on the record today, formally withdraw a motion that was accidentally filed by the Defence yesterday entitled "Dragan Jokic's Amended Requested for Disclosure." We will refile that at another time. But I'd like to on the record, because I can't write a formal written notice to the Court, revoke and withdraw that motion for consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. Can you give me a reason why you can't write such a formal --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, I can next week. I've already packed my computer to go home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have it in the transcript, but please, as it is usual in these cases, please let us know in writing as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will follow up with a written motion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this. Anything additional, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be heard briefly. Michael Karnavas. The issue of disclosure remains, in my opinion, fairly problematic. I understand that the Prosecution is trying to provide us with the disclosure material at a fairly rapid pace. However, they have their limitations, given the need for translation and checking the translation and what have you. Nonetheless, from January, when we first had our status hearing, I mentioned the Butler report. Here we are close to August. Butler is nowhere near. He's vacationing, as I understand it. And I would like to make sure that the Court's remarked today that it should be done by that -- that it's actually an obligation on the OTP to make sure that it is in our hands, because the report itself is only a hundred pages, but the footnotes to the report, the previous one, refer to about a thousand pages, and we need to go over all of that material to make sure that we get to the truth, as the Court is obligated to do so. So that's a critical issue. The other issue, as I understand it, Mr. McCloskey indicated -- he used the word "material witness," and I'm a little confused, because in our motion and in the reply that I filed, based on the leave that I was granted, I believe I made it abundantly clear that our position is that we want everything, their entire file dealing with Srebrenica. And I am insistent on that, Your Honour, because if you look at the indictment and in the way that it is phrased, they have at least Mr. Blagojevic involved from the beginning to the very end. And if we are to get at the truth, then witnesses that they may not believe are material to their case or they may believe are not exculpatory witnesses may indeed have information that is exculpatory or may lead to witnesses that have exculpatory information. Therefore, I want to make sure that I'm very clear on the record that we want the entire Srebrenica file from the Prosecution. And I believe we're entitled to it, based on the joinder indictment that they have proposed to this Tribunal. Now, I may reconsider my position if they somehow amend the indictment based on court orders, but as it stands, I believe that in all due fairness to all of the accused that we should be entitled to the entire file. And with that in mind, I would urge the Court to urge the Prosecution to perhaps hire additional staff, do whatever it needs to do to ensure that they could make the copies well in advance, buy the CDs, whatever it takes, so that we can proceed with all deliberate speed. If we had the discovery -- the disclosure, as I've indicated, we could be ready for trial as early as November. I understand we have some limitations, but the longer it takes for us to get the material, the less prepared we're going to be. And if we're going to get to the truth, then we need to have access to this material. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Before giving the floor to the OTP, I want to emphasise that when we currently ask or request the OTP to do this and that until a concrete date, there is no doubt that the OTP feels obliged under this request to do so. This is true also for the Butler report. As regards the other material, we can't discuss in detail Rule 68 to a certain extent applying -- to be applied correspondingly as regards formal witness statements. I would invite, if necessary, the OTP to comment on the question of the Srebrenica file.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There was no misunderstanding whatsoever what the end of October meant, as you have said. And regarding the discovery, we, of course, under the reciprocal discovery provisions as invoked by three of the four accused, Mr. Karnavas being one of those, we intend to provide the material that may be -- excuse me, the documents and other things described, including witness statements that may be material to the preparation of the defence. That does not say the entire Prosecution file. I don't think Mr. Karnavas is suggesting Rule 70 material is something that he should have. I appreciate that he's giving us a clue on what he feels is material to the preparation, and we will look at this very broadly. And in effect, when you're looking at a large number of documents, it's much simpler for us to interpret it broadly and to give him the broadest possible, as opposed to pick and choose. So the only picking and choosing that we'll do are material such as Rule 70, material that is internal to the Prosecution, certain materials that would be highly confidential under the rules in any investigation. So, I don't expect we have a real problem, and if there's something in particular Mr. Karnavas wants, he and I have always been able to discuss these things. And I don't think we'll have a problem. And when we do, we'll file motions. But I don't see any particular point of litigation right now but -- and we may get there, but we're doing our best to provide full and complete disclosure under the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Indeed, I believe for today, we can leave this with the -- this exchange of views. If there should be in future any dispute, feel free to contact the Trial Chamber directly if you need an order, if you feel not treated in the correct way, and if you believe that there is additional material you really need. So we can't go into any further details, if there is not a question of utmost importance as regards disclosure today. Then I would have one additional question to Mr. Karnavas: What is the position of yours and, of course, your client as regards second Defence counsel in the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We've taken care of that detail, Your Honour. I mean, I assume that -- I assume that you're concerned that we don't have a second counsel at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If -- as I understand the rules, we are entitled to one. We will have one. And I suspect that it will most likely be Ms. Tomanovic that's currently working on the case. So I would not be concerned, I mean, if I were you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That's really nice; but on the other hand, on some experience in previous cases, we appreciate that at the earliest point in time there is a Defence team. And I don't want to ask the accused already today that in case one Defence counsel, for the one or other reason, can't be present - and in these cases we have before us, this will be always the one or other day the case - that the accused agree in writing that they, in the absence of the other Defence counsel, are prepared to continue the case only in the presence of one Defence counsel. This is the underlying reason. And I think this should be done as soon as possible. I hope you will be always present here, Mr. Karnavas, but it may be that also you, the one or other day, want to take, say, holiday or other unexpected things will happen. So it's in the interests of justice to have two Defence counsel, to have an entire Defence team, and that if necessary only one Defence counsel acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I fully appreciate, and I trust that I can count on His Honour to assist me from prying more resources from the Registry, because that's one of the considerations. They have a different view as to how somebody charged with these sorts of allegations should be represented, and the resources are limited. And we're trying to stretch the resources, particularly since the case may go on for another year before we go to trial. But I do understand the Court's position, I respect the Court's position, and obviously we will honour the Court's position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And now you have exactly touched the point why I raised this issue today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then -- please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on behalf of the Defence of Mr. Nikolic, I would like to ask you to bear in mind that he was arrested in April of this year. And with due respect for the fact that the other co-accused were arrested earlier, the Defence counsel for Mr. Nikolic stressed to your legal officer that we do need more time than the others to get prepared for this trial. As far as materials are concerned, we have so far received only the supporting material, 16 or 17 witness statements from the Krstic case. And earlier today, Mr. McCloskey informed us here at the Status Conference that the rest of the materials are pending. Defence for the accused Nikolic intends to invoke Rule 65(B), reciprocal disclosure, that is, and we will do that fairly soon, which will enable us, hopefully, to receive a large volume of materials, including those of the Zvornik and Bratunac Brigades. We will need a lot of time to do that. And to that end, I am kindly asking you to extend the time allocated for preparing pretrial briefs. The time we have now, in our opinion, is too short for us to get prepared for a fair and just defence and proper representation of Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I learned about your concern yesterday, and we discussed it briefly. The rule to be applied here is normally that the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. case should be ready for trial within six months. And taking into account that the necessary documents will be provided to you immediately, I think it's fair enough to expect you to be ready for trial by the end of the year. There is a period of, say, five months for you. And take into account what I said before: Maybe the case can start, worst case, in May. So please proceed in the way that is most appropriate for you. I have no doubts that you will be provided with the necessary material immediately, and try to stick to the schedule as indicated before. I think it's possible. Any other issues for the Pre-Trial Conference? Sorry, for the Status Conference? Then I take the opportunity finally to hand down a decision. It's the decision on the accused Blagojevic's request for judicial notice and deletion of facts from the indictment. The Trial Chamber has decided that this motion is denied. We make reference to the arguments put forward by the OTP. First of all, it should be emphasised that Rule 94(B) applies only to those facts proven beyond a reasonable doubt in other proceedings. Invocation of Rule 94(B) is clearly contingent upon a previously judicial conclusion that such facts are indeed true. Judicial conclusion that certain facts were not proven beyond a reasonable doubt in a previous trial does not suggest that such facts are true or false or provable or not provable. Rather, it simply reflects the other Trial Chamber's opinion that in that particular proceeding, it had not been presented with evidence sufficient to establish those facts beyond a reasonable doubt. Such conclusions by a Trial Chamber are not adjudicated facts within the meaning of Rule 94(B). But I'm quite sure we will come back to Rule 94(B) in another context; at least, I hope so. May we then turn immediately to the hearings on provisional release as regards Mr. Blagojevic and Mr. Obrenovic. The representatives of Mr. Jokic and Mr. Nikolic and the accused Nikolic himself, they are excused for now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may we stay and listen to the proceedings? Can we get your permission to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We were confronted with this question already earlier. And at that time, we decided that it's a matter decided -- only to be decided on an individual basis with respect to the individual applying here for provisional release. And therefore, please understand that we would ask you, if necessary and if you so want, to listen in the public gallery.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to make sure that I understand, you want me gone, too, right? Am I to leave as well? I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, it's very kind. But as I said earlier, we should discuss only this case with the accused and, of course their representatives, in the case we have before us. And this is also the provisional release of your client. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So we are going to handle both at the same time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is fully aware that it's mandatory to have individual decisions because the personal situation of each accused is a different one. But nevertheless, I think we can all agree that certain points are in common, and they should be discussed in this joint hearing on the both motions on provisional release we have before us. We have received not only the motion, the response, we have received the reports on the behaviour of the accused whilst in custody. Therefore, I think we can limit ourselves to the core issues of the question of provisional release. And I would ask also the parties to be as short as possible and to avoid, if possible, repetitions. May the Defence for Mr. Obrenovic - this was the first motion filed - please start.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. On behalf of Mr. Obrenovic, we appreciate the opportunity to appear before the Trial Chamber today in support of his motion for provisional release. I will take into account your instructions just issued that you have read everything, and I certainly will not make any attempt to repeat everything that we have said in our filings. I believe that the filings on behalf of Mr. Obrenovic and also, for that matter, the ones filed by the Prosecution are complete and accurately set forth the opposing views on this issue. The defendant -- the accused, Mr. Obrenovic, fully understands that it is his burden to show that, first of all, he will return for trial as required; and secondly, that he will pose no danger to any witnesses. We have set forth in great detail, or I believe sufficient detail, at any rate, in our motions the reasons why we believe that it is clear that he will return for trial. He has cooperated with the Prosecution, with the Tribunal, and with the United Nations Detention Unit from the time that he became involved in this case. In fact, from well before he became involved in the case, when he was interviewed by the Prosecution months before his arrest. He was also asked by them to provide certain documents and access to certain evidence. He cooperated in those instances. He always appeared voluntarily for the interview sessions that were set for him, and at the close of the second interview, as we have said, it was very clear to Mr. Obrenovic that he was, in all likelihood, going to be indicted. We have set out in our brief his offer to the Prosecution to surrender himself if they would notify him when and where to show up. For five months there was nothing further on the case. He remained at his place of business, his place of work, and at his home, and that's where he was arrested, without incident, some five months after that offer. We appreciate that it is the Prosecution's authority to arrest rather than to honour such requests. There's nothing we can do about that. However, we do believe that the record in this instance should hopefully lead the Trial Chamber to conclude that there are no adverse inferences to be drawn in this instance from Mr. Obrenovic not surrendering himself. He did everything he could do to do so. Since he was arrested, he has cooperated with the Tribunal and with the United Nations Detention Unit. We have cooperated with the Prosecution. I believe and certainly hope that Mr. McCloskey would agree that we have been cooperative in our approach to the case. We have announced to the Court from my very first appearances that we did not intend to contest the uncontestable or contest the things that were not really of importance to us. We have a very straightforward defence in this case, and it is that did he not know about the incidents which were charged in the indictment, nor should he have known, under the circumstances. It is a very complex case. Mr. Obrenovic is quite comfortable with the concept of Your Honours -- as of course he must be, but he is, in truth, comfortable with the concept that Your Honours will make those decisions after you have heard all of the evidence from the Prosecution and all of the evidence from the Defence. That's all we ask for. He, as he said to Mr. McCloskey and to the Office of the Prosecution, at any rate, on the record at his interview, if he is released, he will not run. He has nowhere to go. His family has lived in that Zvornik area and in the Bosnia area for more than 50 years. He comes from a very stable family. He has a wife, children. He's no longer in the military. It's his hope that if he is released on provisional release he can return to Zvornik and help support his family. He has a wife and a 6-year-old son. His absence is a great hardship on them because they, of course, lose his income since he's here. We are very concerned, of course, by the fact that we still don't have a trial date. We understand why we don't have a trial date. We certainly listen to what the Court tells us, and we appreciate the fact that there are so many courtrooms and so forth and that there are other cases also which may get to trial before us. But the bottom line, Your Honour, is that there is an excellent chance that our case will not go to trial for perhaps another year. If that is true, then Mr. Obrenovic, without ever having been convicted of anything, will have spent more than two years in prison before he gets to trial. As the Court has pointed out in numerous decisions, both this Trial Chamber and others, that is not the acceptable standard in most instances and it's not necessary in this case. We would just like to make a couple of points with regard to the Prosecution's brief on this case. They point to Mr. Pandurevic and say Mr. Pandurevic, they believe, is in Serbia. Is he? I don't know. I'm sure they know more about that than we do. And they point out the fact that Mr. Obrenovic could go to Serbia and suddenly remove himself from the jurisdiction of the Court. Now, whether that is true with the situation in Serbia today I think is arguable, but I think the most telling point on this issue is that he did not go to Serbia. We invite the Trial Chamber to compare his situation to Mr. Pandurevic's. Mr. Obrenovic has faced everything responsibly. He has done what everybody has asked him to do. He shows up when people ask him to do so. He answers the questions. He provides physical evidence. And since he has been arrested, he has behaved responsibly at the Detention Unit, as set forth in Mr. McFadden's statement. We would invite you to compare that with the case of Mr. Pandurevic, if Mr. Pandurevic is, in fact, a fugitive. The telling point again is that Mr. Obrenovic is here, and he is here because he stayed at his location and because he has met his responsibilities. So we believe that the argument, the invocation of the Pandurevic spectre that somehow if he's released he's going to do what Mr. Pandurevic did is not a very good argument and not a very persuasive one. He could have done that months before his arrest if that was his intention. He didn't. The proof is in the pudding, as we say in our system, and we believe that in this instance he has established as best he possibly can that he is a responsible person, that he will follow your orders, that he will do exactly what you tell him to do. The second prong of the test which we also understand is that he will not be a danger to any other witness. The Prosecution has filed the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. If you want to address the confidential filed motion of the Prosecution now, then we should go, please, into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Closed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When we are then in public session, I should like the Defence counsel for Mr. Blagojevic to address in the same "to the point" manner the issues especially related to his client.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [No microphone]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think you can wait. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First, I want to thank the Chamber for fast-tracking this request. I think the brief that we presented adequately sets forth what the law is. It's pretty set and concrete. There's no need for me to repeat what's in the brief or to go over material that was so artfully and succinctly put by Mr. Wilson. In looking at the Prosecution's response, paragraph 7, they focus on one aspect, and that is they say that Mr. Blagojevic has not satisfactorily established that he will appear for trial. That's one of the two-pronged requirements. Therefore, I think we can discard any argument that the Prosecution has with respect to Mr. Blagojevic should he be released, will, in any way, shape, or form influence or intimidate in any way witnesses, victims, or other persons. So in essence, as I read their objection to Mr. Blagojevic's provisional release, it's based on that we have not provided or satisfied the first prong. In looking at their response, they then do not, in any concrete fashion, set out as to how it is that we have not satisfactorily established that he will not appear for trial. It's just a blanket statement being made by the Prosecution, as I would expect them to make when not having anything other to argue. This case began with the arrest of Mr. Blagojevic back on August 10th, almost a year ago. He was totally unaware that he had been indicted. He had never been asked to provide a statement. OTP's office in Banja Luka is only 3 to 5 kilometres away, a 5-minute distance. He was totally unaware that he was -- that he was under indictment or that he was a suspect or even a witness, even though he was fully aware that other members of the Drina Corps or the Bratunac Brigade were being questioned at the time, and he was fully aware, as the whole world was aware, that General Krstic was on trial and was convicted and was given a stiff sentence. And yet, never did he leave the RS. He did not try to influence anybody. He did not try to escape to a foreign country. So he was readily available. In fact, part of his job was to have daily contact or occasional contact with SFOR. So to say somehow that now he presents a flight risk, to just make a blanket statement without any concrete evidence, I think, to put it mildly is sheer poppycock. There is nothing there to suggest that he will not return. The Prosecution then goes on to state that because of the severity of the charges, that is a consideration. And obviously, it is. But as we pointed out, there have been other instances in other cases, and I hesitate to mention names, because I don't think it's appropriate, but there have been other instances where accused who are in an advanced age with very serious crimes, in essence, if they were convicted, would die in prison. And that in and of itself is a life sentence. We did point out that this particular Trial Chamber did release accused Jokic. The Prosecutor at the Court's invitation indicated that should he be convicted, he would be facing a 30- or 40-year sentence. At age 45, he would end up getting out at age 85, either -- assuming that he would still be alive in prison. That in and of itself is a life sentence; yet, the Prosecution did not object to Mr. Jokic's release and did not raise this issue, even though when you look at the indictment, you can see that he is prominently in almost every single count, with the exception of the most serious counts of genocide. The Prosecution in paragraph 11 indicates that - and it's a quite clever argument, if I may say - they indicate that they have strong evidence, strong evidence. Now, it is clear from -- and it's established here in the Tribunal that the Trial Chambers will not look at the weakness or the strength of a Prosecution's case in determining whether somebody should be provisionally released. That is available in the United States, for instance. It's codified. But here, there's a two-prong test. And if -- and I suggest that that is exactly what the Prosecution is attempting to do here, is to argue that somehow their case is so strong it's an inevitable conviction; keep him in. If you further read into their motion, it would be clear that what they are saying actually is that as a matter of public policy, anybody charged with genocide or complicity with respect to Srebrenica in genocide should not, as a matter of law, be released, which is clearly impermissible, clearly impermissible. And I think we argued that point quite well in the brief. There is absolutely not one identifiable, concrete piece of evidence refuting the conditions that have been set forth by Mr. Blagojevic in the brief. The Prosecution does not argue, for instance, that the conditions are not strict enough. They do not argue that the RS, the Republika Srpska, is not or has not cooperated, or will not cooperate. They do not argue that somehow he's going to cross over a bridge into a foreign country that has been less than cooperative in the past. They don't argue that he will intimidate any witnesses. It is clear, because of his housing situation, he will be living off base. So he will be living in the city limits. He will be reporting to the police on a daily basis. They will have access at any time or day to go in and make spot checks. The only thing obviously we have requested, and I would be making this request irrespective of this particular hearing, is that we have the opportunity to visit the site, given the importance and complexity of this case, in order for Mr. Blagojevic to assist in the preparation of his Defence, as he is entitled to under the statute and under all the -- international legal instruments upon which the statute was founded. I don't want to belabour the point. I think the conditions that we have set forth, Your Honour, are very clear. These are the same conditions that other Trial Chambers have adopted in other cases. And I think what the Prosecution is attempting to do in a subtle way is to have this Trial Chamber send a message. And it's quite clear, as you have indicated, Mr. President, that this Tribunal is not mandated to sending messages. It's mandated to apply the law. And as a matter of fairness, we believe Mr. Blagojevic should be allowed to be provisionally released because in this case, it smacks of unfairness on the other side. They never contacted him, either as a witness or a suspect. They never gave him the opportunity to provide a statement. They never gave him the opportunity to turn himself in. And once, obviously, he was arrested, he exercised his right to remain silent, and he has a right to do so. Not to mention the way he was arrested, as if he was some sort of drug kingpin, obviously did not put him in the frame of mind to view the Prosecution as if they were there to be fair. So as a matter of fairness, Your Honour, given the fact that you have to look at the totality of the circumstances, I believe that we have met our burden, and the burden should shift on the Prosecution to establish as to how it is they believe we have not established sufficiently that he will appear for trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Before we turn to the Office of the Prosecutor, may I ask the amici curiae from Bosnia and Herzegovina, whether they want to add anything to that what they have given us in writing until now, especially the guarantees? Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Your Honour, thank you for allowing me to speak. I am representing the Government of Republika Srpska at this trial. And as you know, this government has submitted a guarantee. I can, however, state that the government has provided some additional guarantees for Mr. Obrenovic. Unfortunately, due to shortness of time, I cannot offer the same kind of guarantees for Mr. Blagojevic, although I am certain the government would have provided them had I had time to ask for them. With your leave, I will read the additional guarantees which the Government of Republika Srpska has provided for Mr. Obrenovic. They are very brief, and I hope will not take up too much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Until now, it was the custom in this Tribunal to have these guarantees in writing, and I think it's appropriate if you, after this hearing, present the documents to the registry or the senior legal officer in this case sitting before me. I appreciate this. One question: The guarantees as regards Mr. Blagojevic, they date, indeed, 20th of June, 2002? Because it was to a certain surprise to receive these guarantees before the motion on provisional release dated the 17th of July, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I know, the Defence submitted a request to the Government of Republika Srpska asking for a guarantee. As I was able to be present at a government session, and immediately after this session, I arrived in The Hague, I brought the original with me. As you see, the time is very short, or rather the time that has elapsed since the guarantee was issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then let's proceed this way: that additional documents are given to the senior legal officer. Please, your colleague wants to address the Court as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKOVAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, on behalf of the Presidency, I wish only to indicate that our Presidency does not have the required instruments which would enable it to provide guarantees pursuant to requests for provisional release. There is some confusion, because this guarantee was issued by the government, and I'm speaking on behalf of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. I think it's now for the Office of the Prosecutor to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, our responses are in written form, but I would merely and briefly emphasise the foundation of both arguments are a flight risk, and that is because both these men, Commander Blagojevic at the time, and Deputy Commander Obrenovic at the time, were involved in the largest mass execution since World War II, and they will be facing life sentences if they're convicted. At the same time, they live right across the river from Serbia where Vinko Pandurevic, the former colleague of both of them, has been a -- has been hiding out for a long time, as well as others that I don't need to go into at this point. There is no record of them turning themselves in, nor would it have been the obligation of the Prosecutor to allow such men in such circumstances to turn themselves in. The world, unfortunately, is not as nice a place as described by the Defence counsel, and the people in it and the governments in the former Yugoslavia cannot meet the responsibilities that one would expect in a civilised world, and flight risk to Yugoslavia is a very reasonable possibility under all of these circumstances. That is principally what we are founding this argument on, as well as the other argument related to Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May we finally turn to the main persons. It is a question of the ongoing or not ongoing detention, deprivation of liberty, and therefore, I have to ask both Mr. Obrenovic and Mr. Blagojevic, do you want to add anything from your point of view to that what has already been said? Mr. Obrenovic first, please. THE ACCUSED OBRENOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, I wish to thank you for considering my request. I wish to tell you that if you grant my request, I will strictly adhere to any conditions set by you. I will do nothing to hinder the investigation or do anything of that sort and that I will appear at any time and place set by you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to say that any conditions imposed by the Chamber in connection with my possible provisional release, pursuant to my request that I will strictly adhere to those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The Trial Chamber will hand down, as soon as possible, a decision in writing on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that I shouldn't be interrupting you. I just wanted to clarify the matter of the guarantee, because you had that particular question. I might be able to assist you as to why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I understand that you, in preparation of your motion, asked for this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it was only yesterday that the gentleman had the opportunity. But also, we got the guarantee in about five days, which is a record time to start with, because it normally takes two or three months sometimes. So we were trying to fast-track this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for this additional clarification, and the case is adjourned.
